title: Children of the Day: Watchful, Sober, Thankful
summary: The Day of the Lord will come suddenly, like a thief in the night, on people who feel secure. But believers are children of the light, so they are to stay awake and sober, armed with faith, love, and hope, because God has appointed them to salvation, not wrath. Paul then gives a rapid series of instructions for church life (respect leaders, care for the weak, rejoice, pray, give thanks, test prophecy) and closes with a prayer for their complete sanctification and a blessing.
story: Chapter 4 answered a question about believers who had died; chapter 5 answers a related question about when the Lord will come. Paul has already taught them this, so he reminds rather than instructs. His answer is not a date but a way of living: those who belong to the day live as people ready for it. The second half of the chapter brings the whole letter to a close with instructions that turn its themes (faith, love, hope, holiness, and the Lord's coming) into the ordinary habits of a congregation. The final prayer echoes 3:13, drawing the letter's two halves together.
historical:
Paul's teaching about the Day of the Lord drew on the Old Testament prophets, who spoke of a coming day when God would act in judgment and salvation (Amos 5:18-20; Joel 2; Zephaniah 1). Jesus used the picture of a thief coming unexpectedly to describe the Son of Man's coming (Matthew 24:43-44; Luke 12:39-40), and Paul's use of it here suggests that Jesus' sayings were known and taught in the churches very early.

The church had leaders already, only months after its founding: those who work diligently among you, who preside over you in the Lord and give you instruction (verse 12). Their titles are not given, and the offices of elder and overseer familiar from later letters are not named. Paul also mentions prophecies (verse 20), a gift exercised in the early churches, as 1 Corinthians 12 to 14 shows at greater length.
cultural:
The phrase peace and security (verse 3) may echo slogans of Roman imperial propaganda, which celebrated the peace (pax) and security (securitas) that Rome's rule had brought to the world; inscriptions and coins advertised both. Many scholars think Paul is contrasting that confidence with the sudden coming of God's Day, though others see a more general echo of the false prophets' cry of peace when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Night in the ancient city was dark, unpoliced, and associated with drunkenness and crime, which gives force to Paul's contrast between those who belong to the night and those who belong to the day.

The holy kiss (verse 26) was a common greeting among family and friends in the ancient world, and early Christians practiced it as a sign that fellow believers were family. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church, and Paul's solemn charge that this letter be read to all the brothers (verse 27) reflects both that practice and the authority he claimed for his words.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 11 are an exhortation built on contrasts: day and night, light and darkness, awake and asleep, sober and drunk, salvation and wrath. Paul plays on the word sleep, which in chapter 4 meant death and here means moral carelessness; in verse 10, awake or asleep seems to mean living or dead. The armor image in verse 8 draws on Isaiah 59:17, where God puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet, and it gathers the triad of faith, love, and hope from 1:3. Verses 12 to 22 are a rapid string of short commands, some of them only two or three words in Greek, which read almost like a church's rule of life. Verses 23 to 28 close with a prayer, a promise, requests, and a blessing.

outline.t: The Day will come like a thief
Children of the light, awake and sober
Respecting leaders and caring for one another
Rejoice, pray, give thanks, test everything

doctrines.note: The Day of the Lord will bring sudden destruction on those who say peace and security, and they will not escape (verse 3). Judgment is certain and unexpected for those who are not ready. Believers, however, are not appointed to wrath but to salvation (verse 9).

God has appointed believers to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us so that we may live together with him (verses 9 and 10). Salvation is God's appointment, rests on Christ's death, and aims at life with him.

Do not extinguish the Spirit, do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things (verses 19 to 21). Paul neither despises spiritual gifts nor accepts every claim uncritically. Christians differ over whether prophecy continues today, but all can take Paul's pattern of openness with discernment.

The church is a community of mutual care: honoring those who lead, admonishing the idle, encouraging the fainthearted, helping the weak, being patient with everyone, and refusing revenge (verses 12 to 15). Everyone is responsible for everyone.

words.note: Kleptes, thief. The image, which goes back to Jesus (Matthew 24:43), stresses not stealth but surprise: a thief does not announce his arrival. For those who are not ready, the Day will come unexpectedly. For believers, who are children of the day, it will not overtake them like a thief, not because they know the date, but because they are awake.

Adialeiptos, unceasingly or constantly. In ordinary Greek it could describe something that recurs persistently or regularly, not necessarily without any break at all. To pray without ceasing means a life in which prayer returns again and again, not a demand to do nothing else. Paul used the same word of his own prayers for the Thessalonians (1:3; 2:13).

Holokleros, whole or complete in every part. Paul prays that the believer's entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless (verse 23). Some Christians read this as teaching that a human being has three parts, others as a way of saying the whole person, since Scripture elsewhere speaks of people as body and soul. Either way, Paul's concern is that God will sanctify the whole person, including the body.

christ: Christ is the center of the chapter's hope. The Day of the Lord, which the prophets announced as the day of God's coming, is now tied to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (verse 23). Salvation comes through him, and verse 10 is one of the earliest written statements of why he died: “He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him.” His death is for us, in our place and on our behalf, and its goal is shared life with him, which not even death can interrupt. The God of peace will sanctify his people completely, and he will do it because he is faithful (verse 24). The letter ends with the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.
questions: What does it mean in everyday life to stay awake and sober as someone who belongs to the day?
Verses 16 to 18 call believers to rejoice at all times, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in every circumstance. Which of these is hardest for you right now, and why?
Paul tells the church to admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, and help the weak. How do you tell which one a person needs?
